1.reasoning: Genesis 1:6-8 gives the firmament's purpose as separating the waters above from the waters below, and none of the three printed options says this. Only A to C are present, so the correct option (almost certainly a D about separating the waters) seems to have been lost in transcription. The best case for A is that the lights were set in the firmament on day four (Genesis 1:14-17). But the firmament is where the lights were placed, not a source of light itself, and the lights are a separate act of creation. Keying A would teach something the text does not say.

2.reasoning: Genesis 2:17 attaches one consequence to eating from the tree: 'in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.' The prohibition is therefore framed as protection from death. The case for B rests on the tree's name, but the text never presents exposure to evil as the reason for the command. Expulsion (A) came later as a punishment, and living forever (C) belongs to the tree of life. Standard Nigerian CRS texts teach death as the stated sanction.

5.reasoning: Joseph read the dreams as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, then advised storing grain in advance (Genesis 41:33-36). That is foresight and planning, which is what 'visionary' means. Righteous (B) is the strongest alternative since Joseph is a model of integrity elsewhere, but interpreting dreams and advising a storage plan shows foresight, not moral uprightness. Hardworking and affable are not what this episode demonstrates.

6.reasoning: Exodus 2:11-12 says Moses went out to his people and saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, 'one of his people,' and he killed the Egyptian. The point of the episode is his identification with his Hebrew kin, even though he was raised in Pharaoh's court. Upright (B) might be argued as defending the oppressed, but a secret killing followed by hiding the body is not presented as uprightness. D fails because God had not yet called or commanded him.

10.reasoning: Barak would go to battle against Sisera only if Deborah went with him (Judges 4:8). By agreeing, she went into war and led Israel's campaign, which shows courage and leadership. Humility and tolerance (A) might be argued from her accepting Barak's condition, but she answered by warning that the glory would go to a woman, which is not humility. The other pairs have nothing to do with going to war.

11.reasoning: Judges 4:1-3 says Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, so he sold them into the hand of Jabin of Canaan, who oppressed them for twenty years. The oppression was a response to unfaithfulness, and the lesson taught is that God expects obedience and faithfulness. C, God's right to punish through Canaan, is the strongest alternative, but it states a general prerogative rather than the reason, and its wording makes Canaan the agent instead of Israel's sin the cause. A and D have no basis in the text.

13.reasoning: 1 Samuel 8:1-5: the elders said to Samuel, 'you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways; now appoint for us a king.' B restates this exactly. D draws on 8:20, where the people want a king to fight their battles like all the nations, but that is a later addition to the demand, and its wording about nations that 'won battles' is not in the text. A and C wrongly bring Eli in.

22.reasoning: Jezebel's letters told the elders to proclaim a fast and set up two false witnesses, so that Naboth would be condemned for blasphemy under the law and Ahab could then take his vineyard (1 Kings 21:8-16). Her aim was a legal pretext for seizing the vineyard. The strongest case for C is that the letters did order Naboth stoned. However, stoning was the means, not the aim, and the letters named no 'young men'; they called for two base fellows as witnesses. A and D do not match the text.

26.reasoning: Nehemiah 1:3 describes the remnant as being in great affliction and reproach because the walls were broken down, and 2:17 reads 'let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.' The text itself uses the word. Challenge (A) describes how he responded, but the question asks how he saw the ruins, and the text calls them a reproach. Threat and surprise have no textual basis.

28.reasoning: Daniel 3:13 records that Nebuchadnezzar, in furious rage, commanded that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be brought to him. That is his immediate reaction, and D describes it exactly. B is the strongest distractor because the furnace order is the best-known part of the story, but it came only after he questioned them and they refused again (3:14-20). 'Immediate' in the stem is there to rule B out.

33.reasoning: After the miraculous catch of fish in Luke 5:8, Peter fell at Jesus' knees, confessed himself a sinful man, and called him Lord. A sense of one's own sinfulness in someone's presence is a reaction to holiness, so this is a recognition of divinity. Authority (A) is the strongest alternative, since Peter had obeyed Jesus' command to let down the nets. But confessing sin is a response to divine holiness, not to authority. Humanity and kingship do not fit.

34.reasoning: Jesus' demands of discipleship are to deny oneself, take up the cross, count the cost and forsake all (Luke 9:23, 14:25-33). The lessons from these are determination and self-denial, the standard textbook terms. Faith and spiritual maturity (C) are general Christian virtues, but they are not the specific demands in the discipleship passages. A is irrelevant, and D names general virtues that are not the demands.

35.reasoning: In Matthew 18:32-34 the master calls the servant wicked because he had been forgiven yet showed no mercy to his fellow servant, and in anger hands him to the jailers. The grounds for the jailing are his treatment of his fellow servant. The case for C is that he was jailed until he paid the debt, but that debt had already been forgiven and was reinstated only because of his harshness. The debt set the terms of his jailing; his treatment of the fellow servant was the reason for it.

39.reasoning: Both derivers treated the stem as garbled and answered from Jesus' rebuke in Luke 24:25-27, which gives B. However, the stem as printed describes a real event: in Luke 24:18 Cleopas rebukes the stranger: 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there?' Read literally, the inference is that ignorance of public affairs is blameworthy, which matches C, 'political apathy is unpatriotic.' C is too specific to be a random distractor, so it may well be the key the setter wanted. Because a careful student cannot tell whether the setter meant the stem as printed (C) or the more familiar rebuke by Jesus (B), B and C are both defensible.

40.reasoning: Matthew 27:51-52 gives the order: the curtain of the temple was torn in two, then the earth shook, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened. B is the first event. 'Was born' is plainly a typo for 'was torn'; no other reading of 'temple's curtain' makes sense, so the question can still be answered. A, the earthquake, is the strongest alternative because it is the most dramatic event, but Matthew puts it after the tearing of the curtain.

44.reasoning: At Pentecost (Acts 2) the apostles preached boldly, about three thousand accepted Jesus as Messiah and were baptized, the church was born, and evangelism began. Fear is the opposite of the outcome, so A is the one option not related to it. The only argument for another option would be that 'birth of the church' is a later label, but Nigerian CRS texts teach it as a standard outcome of Pentecost.

46.reasoning: James 2:8 defines the royal law as 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself,' set against partiality toward the rich. Being each other's keeper is the standard textbook paraphrase of love of neighbour. B is the strongest alternative since loving enemies is also love, but it comes from a different teaching (Luke 6:27), and James 2 is about showing no partiality among fellow believers. A and C have nothing to do with the royal law.

50.reasoning: D is well supported: 1 Peter 1:6-7 and 5:10 teach that suffering lasts 'a little while' and ends in eternal glory. A is just as clearly Petrine teaching on enduring suffering: 1 Peter 2:21 says 'Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example,' and 4:1 says 'since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought.' The stem, 'endure suffering in faith, conscious of the fact that,' fits either ground, and Nigerian CRS texts list both as reasons Peter gives. D is fuller and may be the setter's key, but a well-prepared student could not rule A out as wrong.
